result:
**Read it if you're building a SKILL.md linter or rubric; skip it if you want evidence that these smells hurt agent performance.**

What it is: 238 popular SKILL.md files from the skills.sh marketplace, coded into a 13/44-component taxonomy, plus 26 "smells" derived by inverting community best practices scraped from 29 web sources.

Findings: >99% of files have at least one smell, averaging 10.5; only one file is clean. Rationalization Loophole (nothing stops the agent skipping steps) hits 94%. Task sections appear in 74% of files, Introduction 64%, everything below Practice under 25%. Smells accumulate over a skill's life rather than getting fixed. Six of the 13 component types have no community guidance at all.

The reusable part is the detector design: 5 smells are pure static checks (word/char caps, backslash paths, XML in frontmatter), the other 21 go to an LLM judge prompted per-smell with a definition, one positive and one negative example, and a binary answer. Weighted F1 0.78 on 53 hand-labeled files with a 4-bit quantized Qwen3.6-27B.

Main limitation: the best practices are majority-voted folklore, never causally validated. The paper shows smells are common, not that they cause bad agent behavior. The sample is also biased toward popular public marketplace skills, and the 0.78 F1 rests on 53 labels and one quantized model.

Practical read: skim "What they did" and the smell catalog, take the static/judge split and judge prompt format, ignore the prevalence numbers unless you need a baseline. Full paper adds little beyond the note. arXiv:2607.01456
